newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin, rivals move against him.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin, rivals move against him.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin returned unexpectedly to the Kremlin on Wednesday, shortly before parliament was due to debate a motion on forcing him to step down because of ill health.
"President Yeltsin arrived at the Kremlin at 11.30 this morning (0830 GMT)," a Kremlin spokesman said.
Yeltsin arrived in his office just two days after leaving hospital following 12 days treatment for double pneumonia and went to an official residence outside Msocow to convalesce.
He later met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the Kremlin, Itar-Tass news agency said.

Yeltsin's doctors have expressed concern that the 65-year-old president is trying to do too much too soon. But he is clearly worried that his illness, so soon after heart surgery in November, could play into his rivals' hands.

The State Duma, or lower house of parliament, was due later on Wednesday to debate a motion on forcing Yeltsin to step down on health grounds. The president spent six months out of the Kremlin last year with heart problems, raising doubts over his ability to rule the vast country of 150 million people.
"Either we agree to Russia's collapse or try to do something about it," communist Viktor Ilyukhin, who initiated the motion, told reporters.
Yeltsin loyalists said the Duma appeared to be testing the water for radical political changes which they said could amount to a state coup.

"The opposition is like a child trying to work out whether an object is hot or cold by prodding it with a stick," Interfax news agency quoted Sergei Belyaev, head of the pro-government "Our Home is Russia" faction, as saying.
"The opposition may feel that it has already cooled down, and there's no risk of burning itself, and maybe it will burn itself deliberately to put itself in hospital."
Parliament's own legal department has already cast doubts on the motion, launched after Yeltsin was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8.
The legal experts have said the motion cannot be used to oust the president, who has big powers under the constitution.

Nikolai Ryzhkov, a former Soviet prime minister and a communist ally, said the motion violated the constitution and that the Duma should instead prepare laws to clarify procdures for removing a president because of ill health.
The Kremlin's chief doctor said on Tuesday that Yeltsin, who has not been seen in public since he came down with the illness, was perfectly capable of ruling the country.
"He's in a completely satisfactory condition," Sergei Mironov told Reuters shortly after seeing Yeltsin at the Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow.

Opposition politicians blame Yeltsin's absence for a host of problems dogging Russia, including long delays in state pension and wage payments. Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin were expected to discuss the wages and pension problems during their talks.

Parliament, meanwhile, also planned to target the Swiss diplomat who is overseeing post-war elections in Russia's rebel Chechnya region on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The chamber's international affairs committee has accused Tim Guldimann, head of the OSCE's Chechnya mission, of violating the constitution by helping to fund the January 27 poll.
In an interview with Reuters in the Chechen capital Grozny, Guldimann said on Tuesday he was doing nothing illegal.
